system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2156-04-22 18:00:00 to 2156-04-30 21:13:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, type 2 diabetes, cardiomyopathy due to Chagas disease, and a history of coronary artery bypass grafting presented during a dialysis session with hypotension and bradycardia. He was found to have severe hyperkalemia with a potassium level of 8.6, leading to an idioventricular rhythm. He was treated in the emergency department with calcium gluconate, insulin, dextrose, and atropine, and underwent emergent hemodialysis, which normalized his potassium. His bradycardia and hypotension resolved, and he was weaned off dopamine. His home lisinopril dose was reduced to 20 mg daily to minimize potassium elevation risk. He reported mild diarrhea and possible missed medications prior to admission. Blood cultures showed no growth, and chest imaging revealed stable pleural effusions without signs of infection. He recovered well, restarted his insulin regimen, and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to complete all dialysis sessions and monitor weight.

INDICATION:  ___ male with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis,
now with fever, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and cough for four days. 
Evaluate for pneumonia.

COMPARISON:  ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Frontal and lateral chest radiographs were obtained.

FINDINGS:  Bilateral pleural effusions, right greater than left, are again
seen and grossly unchanged.  There is compressive atelectasis.  Linear
scarring in the left upper lobe is unchanged.  There is no pneumothorax. 
Median sternotomy wires are again seen.  Heart size is slightly enlarged, most
notably in the region of the right atrium.

IMPRESSION:  Persistent bilateral pleural effusions, right greater than left. 
Right atrial enlargement.

INDICATION:  ___ male with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis,
now with fever, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and cough for four days. 
Evaluate for appendicitis.

COMPARISON:  ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Axial CT images through the abdomen and pelvis were acquired after
administration of intravenous contrast.  Coronal and sagittal reformatted
images were reviewed.

FINDINGS:

CT OF THE ABDOMEN WITH IV CONTRAST:  Bilateral pleural effusions are again
seen, right greater than left, with compressive atelectasis.  Heart size is
top normal with right atrial enlargement.  The liver is hypoenhancing and
heterogeneous which may suggest fatty infiltration, although congestive heart
failure may partially contribute to this appearance.  The spleen is grossly
unremarkable.  The patient is status post cholecystectomy and surgical clips
are seen in the gallbladder fossa.  The pancreas is markedly atrophic. 
Calcification at the pancreatic head is again seen and may represent sequela
of prior pancreatitis.  The adrenal glands are unremarkable.  The kidneys are
atrophic bilaterally.  The stomach and visualized loops of small and large
bowel are grossly unremarkable.  Small amount of intraperitoneal fluid is
again seen and appears unchanged.

CT OF THE PELVIS WITH IV CONTRAST:  The bladder is partially decompressed and
therefore incompletely evaluated but grossly unremarkable.  The seminal
vesicles and prostate are grossly unremarkable.  There is no free fluid.  Few
colonic diverticula do not demonstrate inflammation.  The appendix is normal.

Visualized bony structures are grossly unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:  No CT evidence for acute intra-abdominal process.  Stable trace
ascites.  Liver heterogeneity which may be secondary to congestion,
particularly in the setting of right atrial enlargement.  Bilateral pleural
effusions, right greater than left persist.

brachial graft with gram-positive bacteremia.  Please rule out graft abscess
or perigraft fluid collection.

FINDINGS:  The antecubital to axillary graft is patent with arterial
anastomotic velocities of 267 cm/sec.  The venous outflow velocities are 184

The upper arm portion of the graft appears well incorporated without any
evidence of perigraft fluid.  Over a 5-6 cm length near the arterial
anastomosis just above the antecubital fossa, there is some perigraft edema
present with thickening.  There is no discrete abscess.  This may be
consistent with early graft infection.

IMPRESSION:  Patent left brachial axillary AV graft.  The antecubital portion
of the graft has perigraft edema without discrete fluid collection.  This may
represent early or focal graft infection.

FINDINGS:  Compared to most recent prior exam, lung volumes are slightly

INDICATION:  ___ man with end-stage renal disease, for placement of
temporary hemodialysis catheter.

RADIOLOGIST:  Dr. ___ performed the procedure.  Dr. ___,
the attending radiologist was present and supervising throughout.

ANESTHESIA:  1% lidocaine was used for local anesthesia.  50 mcg of fentanyl
was given IV.  Patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously monitored
throughout the procedure.

PROCEDURE AND FINDINGS:  After explaining the risks, benefits and alternatives
of the procedure written informed consent was obtained.  Patient was brought
to the angiography suite and placed supine on the imaging table.  The right
side of the neck was prepped and draped in standard sterile fashion.
Preprocedure timeout and huddle were performed per ___ protocol.

Ultrasound scan of the right side of the neck revealed an occluded right
internal jugular vein.  The right external jugular vein was widely patent and
seen communicating with subclavian vein.  Under ultrasound guidance external
jugular vein was accessed with hard copy images on file using a micropuncture
needle through which a 0.018 guidewire was advanced into the ___.  Needle was
exchanged for a micropuncture sheath and the wire upsized to ___ wire.
After making appropriate measurements the ___ wire was advanced into the IVC
for stability. Micropuncture sheath was removed and the soft tissue tract
dilated using 8, 10, 12 and 14 ___ dilators.  14 ___ x 20 cm temporary
hemodialysis catheter was advanced over the ___ wire.  Tip of the catheter
was positioned in the right atrium.  The guidewire was removed.  Both ports
aspirated and flushed easily.  A final fluoroscopic chest film was obtained
and stored digitally.  Catheter was secured to the skin using 0 silk sutures
and sterile dressings were applied.

The patient tolerated the procedure well and there were no immediate
complications.

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated placement of 14.5 ___ x 20 cm temporary
hemodialysis catheter via right external jugular vein.  Tip of the catheter
terminates in the right atrium and is ready to use.

REASON FOR EXAMINATION:  End-stage renal disease.  Low ejection fraction after
arteriovenous fistula removal, currently with shortness of breath and
pulmonary edema.

Portable AP chest radiograph was reviewed in comparison to ___.

The right central venous line has been inserted for dialysis purposes, with
its tip being at the cavoatrial junction.  Cardiomediastinal silhouette is
unchanged.  There is minimal interval progression of vascular engorgement but
no overt pulmonary edema is seen.  Bilateral loculated effusions and areas of
atelectasis are unchanged.  No pneumothorax is seen.

CLINICAL INDICATION:  ___ male with end-stage renal disease, on
hemodialysis, needs tunneled hemodialysis placement.  Patient has an
indwelling right external jugular venous temporary line which needs to be
tunneled.

CLINICIANS:  Dr. ___ and Dr. ___.  The attending, Dr.
___, was present and supervising during the entire procedure.

1% buffered lidocaine was used for local anesthesia.  Also, lidocaine mixed
with epinephrine was used in the subcutaneous tissue during tunneling. 
Patient was moderately sedated with 75 mcg of fentanyl and 1.5 mg of Versed in
divided doses throughout the total intraservice time of 35 minutes, during
which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously monitored by a
trained radiological nurse.

PROCEDURE DETAILS:  Outlining the risks and benefits of the procedure, a
written informed consent was obtained.  The patient was brought to the
angiography suite and placed supine on the imaging table.  A pre-procedure
timeout and huddle was performed per ___ protocol.  The indwelling
right-sided catheter was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion
including the right upper anterior chest wall.

The scout image of the chest demonstrated the indwelling temporary
hemodialysis catheter with tip ending in the right atrium.  The securing
sutures at the skin were cut.  Both the ports were aspirated and flushed. 
Amplatz wire was then passed through one of the ports and attempts were made
to cannulate the IVC which were unsuccessful.  The Amplatz wire was then left
in situ within the catheter with tip in the right atrium.

Attention was then directed at creating a subcutaneous tunnel.  Appropriate
catheter length measurements were made using the indwelling catheter.  After
infiltrating the subcutaneous and the skin with lidocaine, a 1 cm transverse
skin ___ was made at the right upper anterior chest wall, through which the
permanent hemodialysis catheter measuring 15 ___ x 23 cm cuff-to-tip was
then tunneled towards the venotomy site from where it was brought out.  The
cuff was retracted well within the subcutaneous tunnel.  The Amplatz wire was
then exchanged for the braided J wire was provided in the hemodialysis
catheter kit which was used to cannulate the IVC.  Over this wire, the
indwelling catheter was gently pulled out.  Over this wire, a 15 ___
peel-away sheath was then placed with tip in the right atrium.  Through this
peel-away sheath, the hemodialysis catheter was threaded in, and the peel-away
sheath was peeled out.  The venotomy site was then closed with ___ Vicryl
subcuticular sutures.  The catheter was secured at the skin with 0 silk
sutures and sterile dressings applied.  Both the ports were flushed and
aspirated easily and sterile caps were placed.  Final fluoroscopic scout image
demonstrated the tip to be within the right atrium.  There are no kinks or
malalignment in the tube.  The patient withstood the procedure well and had no
immediate complications and was shifted to the floor in stable conditions with
POE orders.

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated conversion of a temporary right external jugular
hemodialysis line to a tunneled hemodialysis line(23 cm cuff to tip).  The
line is ready for use.

procedures.long_title: Removal of arteriovenous shunt for renal dialysis

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been feeling unwell. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve had fever for a few days now, and I’ve been nauseous, throwing up twice. My stomach hurts all over, kind of like when I had pancreatitis before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any diarrhea or changes in bowel habits?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no diarrhea. Just the pain, nausea, and fever. I also didn’t take my insulin yesterday—my blood sugar’s been running high, in the 300s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks for letting me know. We’ll check your blood sugar and start some fluids. I also noticed you have a dialysis graft in your arm—any pain or redness there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Now that you mention it, yes—my left arm near the graft has been sore and a bit warm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’re going to run some blood tests and get a CT scan to check your abdomen. But the redness and pain at the graft site could mean an infection, which might explain your fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection? From the graft? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially since you’re on dialysis. If bacteria get into the bloodstream from the graft, it can spread. We’ll start antibiotics just in case and get more tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work came back. Your white count is a bit high, and we found something concerning—your blood cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Staph? Like a skin infection? But I don’t have a wound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we suspect the infection is coming from your AV graft. The bacteria likely entered through the skin around it and got into your blood. This is called bacteremia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on an antibiotic called vancomycin. But because the graft is infected, we’ll likely need to remove it. We also did an ultrasound of the graft, and there’s some swelling around it, which supports infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Remove it? But I need it for dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I know. We’ll place a temporary dialysis catheter—first in your neck—so you can keep getting dialysis. Then, once the infection clears, you can get a new graft.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as I can keep dialysis going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your repeat blood cultures are still positive for Staph. It’s the same strain, methicillin-sensitive—MSSA. That’s good news because it means we have effective antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotic is working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should be, but since the bacteria are still in your blood, it means the source—your graft—is still infected. That’s why we need to remove it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning. First, we’ll place the temporary dialysis line in your neck under ultrasound guidance. Then, the surgical team will remove the graft.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated for the line placement, and you’ll get pain medication. The surgery is done under anesthesia, so you won’t feel anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well yesterday. The temporary dialysis catheter was placed in your external jugular vein—no complications. You’re already on dialysis with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. How’s my arm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The graft was removed. We sent a sample from it, and it also grew MSSA—confirms the infection was coming from there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So now we just wait for the antibiotics to clear it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re switching from vancomycin to cefazolin—a better antibiotic for MSSA that’s easier on your kidneys. You’ll get it IV during dialysis, three times a week, for four weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Four weeks? That’s a long time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know, but it’s important to fully clear the infection. If we stop early, it could come back or spread to your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart? Could it affect that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Bacteria can attach to heart valves and cause endocarditis. So we did an echocardiogram. Good news—it didn’t show any infection on your heart valves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your white count is coming down. That means the antibiotics are working. But you’re a bit short of breath—any chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No chest pain, just a little harder to breathe, especially lying down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some fluid buildup, likely from your heart not pumping as well. We’ll adjust your fluids with dialysis and keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart’s weak already, from Chagas. I hope this doesn’t make it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. Your ejection fraction was around 35-40% on echo—better than your baseline of 25%. So your heart is actually doing okay right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures from this morning are negative—great sign! The bacteria are clearing from your blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Does that mean I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re on the right track. We’ll keep the antibiotics going for the full four weeks to be safe, but you’re responding well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my dialysis access?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the temporary catheter for now. Once you finish antibiotics, the transplant team will evaluate you for a new graft.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs continue to improve. Sodium is up, kidney function stable on dialysis. We’re planning to switch your temporary line to a tunneled catheter tomorrow—it’s more secure for longer use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a big procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s minor. They’ll tunnel the catheter under your skin to reduce infection risk. You’ll be sedated, and it takes about 30 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tunneled catheter was placed successfully yesterday. No issues. You’re doing well overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Fever’s gone, stomach pain is better, and I can eat again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’re going to discharge you tomorrow. You’ll continue cefazolin during dialysis for four weeks total, starting from when we removed the graft.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your usual—insulin, blood pressure meds, cholesterol pill. We’re adding tramadol and Tylenol for pain as needed. And carvedilol dose was lowered to 12.5 mg twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why lower the carvedilol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been on the lower side. We want to avoid dizziness, especially with your heart condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’re ready to go home. Keep taking the antibiotics with dialysis, watch your weight—call if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And follow up with my doctors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—your primary doctor, transplant team, and infectious disease. They’ll check your labs weekly and make sure the infection stays gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the care. I feel lucky to be on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, type 2 diabetes, and cardiomyopathy due to Chagas disease presented with fever, nausea, vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain. He was found to have MSSA bacteremia originating from an infected left arm AV graft, which showed signs of cellulitis. Blood and wound cultures confirmed methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. He was started on vancomycin, then transitioned to cefazolin, and underwent removal of the infected graft. A temporary dialysis catheter was placed in the right external jugular vein, later converted to a tunneled catheter. Repeat blood cultures became negative, and his clinical condition improved. He was discharged home on a four-week course of IV cefazolin administered during dialysis, with close outpatient follow-up planned with infectious disease, transplant, and primary care teams.
